summaries.example: Imagine saying, “The sun is going to bed,” when you really mean that evening is coming. You are not claiming the sun is a person. You are using a helpful way of speaking. A fictionalist asks whether some other kinds of talk—perhaps talk about numbers—work in a similar way.
summaries.summary: Fictionalism is the idea that some kinds of speech may work more like useful stories than like ordinary reports of literal facts. A fictionalist might say that people talk about numbers, possible worlds, moral properties, or other subjects in a way that helps them reason, even if the things mentioned are not literally part of reality. The view comes in several forms. Some versions describe what speakers already do; others recommend a new practice. Some focus on language, while others make claims about what exists. Philosophers discuss whether fictionalism can preserve the useful jobs done by mathematics, science, or moral talk without requiring belief in all the entities those subjects seem to mention. They also ask whether these kinds of talk really resemble fiction and whether fictionalism can explain how sentences work together. The entry presents reasons for and against the view rather than settling the dispute.
key_ideas: Fictionalism says that some areas of talk may be useful without aiming at literal truth.
A person might think that numbers do not really exist but still use numbers to count, measure, and solve problems.
Fictionalism can be about language, about what exists, or about both—but those are different questions.
Some fictionalists describe our attitude as pretending or making-believe; others choose weaker ideas, such as accepting a theory without believing it.
Supporters say fictionalism may avoid difficult commitments about what exists. Critics ask whether ordinary talk really feels like pretending and whether the view explains enough.
There are two important choices: describing how people already speak, or recommending a new way they should speak.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fictionalism helps us ask an important question: must a way of talking be literally true in every detail to be useful? It also shows why language and existence should not be confused. We may use a word or idea successfully while still debating what, if anything, it refers to. Thinking about this can make us more careful about science, mathematics, stories, and everyday explanations.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical view that some claims are best understood as useful story-like talk rather than as attempts to state literal facts.
The exact, word-for-word meaning a sentence has in a situation.
A made-up story or pretend way of speaking that can still help us think or communicate.
A claim about what exists, or what kinds of things there are.
A view about how people actually use a kind of talk, rather than a rule about how they should use it.
A view saying that people ought to use a kind of talk in a pretend or story-like way because doing so may be useful.

questions_to_think_about: Can a story or pretend idea help us learn something real?
When you use a phrase like “the sun rises,” are you trying to describe everything exactly?
Could people use numbers successfully even if philosophers disagreed about whether numbers exist?
Would using a helpful fiction be different from making a mistake?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “There are two apples,” while discussing a nominalist view that does not accept numbers as independently existing objects. A fictionalist might say that, in ordinary life, the speaker is using number discourse in a fictional spirit: the statement communicates something useful about the apples, although it need not commit the speaker to numbers as entities. In a philosophy seminar, however, the same sentence might be intended literally. This illustrates use fictionalism, the idea that a sentence can have a literal use that differs from its ordinary, nonliteral use.
summaries.summary: Fictionalism is a family of views about discourses whose apparent commitments may be philosophically controversial. Its provisional idea is that claims in a domain need not be understood as straightforward attempts to describe literal reality; they may function as useful fiction, pretense, metaphor, or another nonbelief-based practice. The entry separates several dimensions that are often run together. A linguistic thesis concerns what utterances do, whereas an ontological thesis concerns what exists. Hermeneutic fictionalism describes how a discourse is actually used; revolutionary fictionalism recommends using it in a nonliteral way. Use fictionalism allows a contrast between ordinary fictional use and occasional literal use, while meaning fictionalism treats the fictional role as built into meaning itself. Further distinctions concern content—what is put forward—and force—whether the speaker asserts, pretends, presupposes, or performs another act. Arguments for fictionalism appeal to antirealist worries, the possibility that an oracle could remove ontological belief without changing our practice, puzzles about existence, and analogies with metaphor or context-sensitive speech. Objections challenge its psychological fit, semantic systematicity, paraphrases, treatment of incomplete fictions, and ability to preserve inference. The broader significance is that fictionalism complicates arguments from ordinary language or scientific indispensability to the existence of the entities mentioned.
key_ideas: Fictionalism is not one single doctrine. It can concern linguistic use, ontology, meaning, speech acts, or mental attitudes.
Hermeneutic fictionalism describes actual practice; revolutionary fictionalism proposes a practice. The two require different arguments.
Use fictionalism differs from meaning fictionalism. The first allows a literal use; the second denies that literal use is available in the relevant way.
Different fictionalists analyze an utterance as pretending, reporting what a fiction says, describing the real world indirectly, or using representational figures.
A major motivation is to avoid widespread error or unwanted ontological commitments while preserving the practical value of a discourse.

Objections include the thought that mathematics or morality does not feel like make-believe, difficulties explaining systematic language, and worries that paraphrases or fictional translations do not preserve logical relations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fictionalism connects metaphysics with philosophy of language. It asks whether apparent reference and ontological commitment can come apart, and whether useful reasoning requires literal belief. These questions matter for mathematics, science, morality, modality, fictional characters, ordinary objects, and other discourses discussed by philosophers. The view also cautions against treating ordinary sentences as simple evidence for what exists: before drawing an ontological conclusion, we may need to understand how the sentences are used and what speakers are doing with them.

important_terms.definition: A strategy holding that claims in a domain are not best understood as aiming at literal truth, but as functioning in a story-like, pretend, or otherwise nonliteral manner.
A thesis about how sentences are used: speakers may communicate or perform an act other than literal assertion when using a discourse.
A thesis about what exists or what ontological status the entities of a discourse have. It can be held separately from a linguistic thesis.
The claim that a discourse is already used nonliterally, even when speakers appear to aim at literal truth.
The recommendation that a discourse ought to be conducted nonliterally because it can serve useful purposes without literal truth.
The view that ordinary utterances have a literal use, but are often used in a fictional spirit instead.
The view that the relevant sentences cannot meaningfully be used literally outside the fiction; their fictional role is part of their meaning.
A debate about what speakers put forward, how they use sentences, and whether they believe, pretend, accept, or presuppose the contents involved.

questions_to_think_about: If a discourse is useful but not literally true, what exactly is the speaker asserting?
Does continuing to use mathematics after learning that numbers do not exist support hermeneutic fictionalism, or merely show that mathematical language is flexible?
Can a fictionalist explain the difference between meaning a sentence and using it in a particular context?
Should a theory be judged partly by the useful work it allows us to do, even if it rejects literal truth?
Could a fictionalist account avoid the same problems faced by paraphrase-based theories?

summaries.example: A class says, “The average student in our school has two siblings.” No one expects there to be one particular student who is the average student. The phrase may help summarize information without naming a real object. A fictionalist uses cases like this to ask whether some mathematical or philosophical talk also works as a useful way of organizing facts rather than as talk about special objects. A critic may reply that “average student” has a different kind of meaning, so the comparison may not prove fictionalism.
summaries.summary: Fictionalism is a family of philosophical views about language and reality. In a fictionalist approach, a discourse may be valuable even when its sentences are not best understood as literal descriptions of what exists. For example, a fictionalist about mathematics might think that ordinary mathematical speech is a useful practice, while remaining unconvinced that numbers are real objects. The entry emphasizes that several distinctions matter. A linguistic fictionalist makes a claim about how sentences are used; an ontological fictionalist makes a claim about the entities the sentences seem to mention. Hermeneutic fictionalism describes current speech, while revolutionary fictionalism recommends a new way to speak. There is also a difference between saying that speakers use sentences fictionally and saying that the sentences can only have fictional meaning. Fictionalists may appeal to pretending, metaphor, acceptance, or another attitude that is weaker or different from belief. Supporters argue that the view can avoid massive error if a discourse has no literal objects, and can preserve useful reasoning. Critics question whether these discourses resemble fiction, whether the account can explain the systematic structure of language, and whether its alternative paraphrases preserve the logical relationships among sentences.
key_ideas: Fictionalism is a group of related positions, not one simple claim that everything is made up.
A person can accept the linguistic idea without accepting the ontological idea, or accept one without the other.
Hermeneutic fictionalism asks what speakers actually do; revolutionary fictionalism asks what they ought to do.
Some versions say speakers pretend, some say they communicate a different content, and some say they accept a theory without believing it literally.
Mathematical fictionalism is motivated partly by the wish to use mathematics without committing to numbers as independently existing things.
Critics argue that ordinary mathematical or moral thinking may not feel like fiction and that fictionalism must still explain meaning, inference, and communication.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fictionalism encourages us to separate three questions: What does a sentence mean? How is it being used? What exists? Those questions often seem to have the same answer, but fictionalism argues that they may come apart. This matters whenever people rely on a useful framework—such as mathematics, scientific models, or talk about possibilities—while debating whether the framework describes independent things in the world.

important_terms.definition: The view that some statements are better understood as useful pretend-talk or story-like talk than as claims meant to be literally true.
A claim about how a kind of language is used, especially whether speakers are making literal assertions or using a nonliteral practice.
A claim about what exists and what sort of existence the entities mentioned in a discourse have.
The position that people already use a discourse in a fictional or pretend-like way, even if it seems literal.
The position that people should adopt a fictional or pretend-like use because the discourse can still accomplish valuable goals.
The idea that a sentence may be used fictionally in ordinary settings but literally in another setting, such as a philosophy discussion.
The idea that the sentences have no meaningful literal use outside their fictional role.
A mental stance such as belief, acceptance, pretense, or indifference toward what a sentence says.

questions_to_think_about: Is using a convenient model the same as believing the model describes reality exactly?
Why might someone want to keep using mathematics while denying that numbers exist?
What difference would it make if a sentence had a fictional use but also a literal use?
Can an analogy with stories or metaphors explain every part of a serious theory?
What should a philosophical theory explain besides whether its claims are useful?
